title: A (Slightly) Dangerous But Effective Way To Get Your Students' Attention
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin shares an unconventional attention-getting technique he has used for years but hesitated to publish: standing on a sturdy chair while giving the standard attention signal during especially loud or active class activities. He explains that the novelty and added height cut through commotion more effectively than the usual method alone, prompting faster and more focused attention. Linsin is careful to frame this as an optional tool for urgent moments only, paired with explicit safety caveats — using the same trusted, sturdy chair every time and never attempting it on an unstable one. He closes by noting that the strategy should not be repeated too often to retain its impact, and adds a postscript reminding teachers to make clear to students that the technique is a teaching tool, not something for them to imitate. The tone is playful but the underlying advice about breaking through classroom noise for genuinely urgent messages is practical.
points: For urgent moments during loud, high-energy activities, adding physical novelty — standing on a sturdy chair while giving the normal attention signal — can cut through commotion faster than the standard method alone.
The strategy should only be used occasionally so the added novelty and urgency don't wear off.
Safety is essential: use the same trusted, solid four-legged chair or stool every time, and never attempt it on an unstable seat.
The added height signals to students, almost instinctively, that something important is about to be said.
Teachers should clarify to students that this is a teaching tool only and not something students should imitate themselves.
quotes: Okay, so I’ve got this strategy I’ve been using a long time. But I’ve been reluctant to share it. Because, you see, it can, potentially anyway, be an eensy-weensy bit dangerous.
But if you add this one little (slightly) dangerous part to it, and don’t use it too often, you can bring an extra layer of urgency to your message.
There is something about the added height—the novelty or whimsicalness of it—that causes students to understand innately that you have something important to tell them.

Now, it’s important to reiterate that you should never jump up on just any chair in the spur of the moment. Check beforehand to make sure that the one you choose is stable, sturdy, reliable, can hold your weight, etc.
I feel comfortable using the strategy and always have. But please, if you decide to try it, be careful. I'd be horrified if videos of teachers losing their balance started popping up on YouTube.
It probably goes without saying, but it’s a good idea to remind your students that the strategy is a teaching tool only, and they may not repeat the practice.
